title: A Detailed Explanation of “Record of Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation-Samādhi”
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: The essay “Record of Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation-Samādhi” is preserved in Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, Volume Four. It is the original manuscript of Master Liaoyu, revised by Master Yinguang before publication, and therefore embodies Master Yinguang’s own experience and insight in cultivating Buddha-recitation-samādhi as well. It is a rare and precious document within the practice of Buddha-recitation. It sets forth in depth the method, the stages, the marks, the function, the essence, and the benefits of Buddha-recitation-samādhi, and in its latter half explains how, once Buddha-recitation-samādhi has been attained, one should carry on the work of preserving the realization.

blocks.text: Record of Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation-Samādhi (Original Text)

inline.s: Master Yinguang
(Master Liaoyu’s original manuscript, lightly revised; because a few sentences were misprinted in the Buddhist Study Miscellany, the original text is recorded here.)

In the year bingwu I shut myself away in retreat at Baoqing Temple in Cixi, cutting off all worldly ties and devoting myself to the pure karmic practice. It happened that the abbot invited Master Dixian to lecture on Master Lianchi’s Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra, just next door to my retreat. So I imitated the old story of Kuang Heng, who bored through a wall to borrow his neighbor’s light, and opened a small aperture in the wall of my cell, so that without leaving my retreat I might attend the lectures at any time. From then on my Buddha-recitation felt ever more intimate: once the Buddha’s name was raised, deluded thoughts vanished completely. A coolness permeated my whole being, and joy filled my heart, just like sweet dew poured over my crown, like the finest ghee enriching my mind. The bliss of it cannot be put into words.

One day a visitor came to my retreat and asked: “I have already practiced the method of Buddha-recitation for more than twenty years. In giving rise to faith, making vows, and undertaking the practice, I have not been insincere; yet my karma is deep and my hindrances heavy, and I have never reached the state of single-mindedness. Judging my own faculties, I am fit only for attaining rebirth while still carrying my karma. Though Buddha-recitation-samādhi is not something I dare hope for in this life, the method by which it may be attained, and the marks by which its attainment is known—Master, please explain these to me.”

I replied: “The states and marks of samādhi are known only to one who has realized them, as when a person drinks water and alone knows for himself whether it is cold or warm. Since I have not realized it, how could I expound it?”
The visitor pleaded again and again without cease.

I replied: “As for the method itself, one must, at the very moment of reciting, turn the recitation back into contemplation, focusing intently upon a single object and never letting the mind wander outward. Thought after thought tends the source of mind; mind after mind accords with the Buddha-essence. Recitation returns to the recitation itself; contemplation returns to the contemplation itself. The reciting is the contemplating, and the contemplating is the reciting. One must bring it about that the whole of the recitation is contemplation, with no contemplation apart from the recitation; and the whole of the contemplation is recitation, with no recitation apart from the contemplation.
Though contemplation and recitation are already blended like water and milk, the root has not yet been interrogated to the bottom. You must take that single
(here meaning “this”)

thought of ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’ and investigate it again and again, rousing yourself to it with all earnestness. The more you investigate, the more urgent it becomes; the more you rouse yourself, the more intimate it becomes. When your strength reaches its utmost and your practice is pure, suddenly the recitation falls away along with the one reciting, and you realize the state of no-thought and yet no absence of thought. This is what is meant by the saying: “The luminous spirit shines alone, utterly freed from the faculties and their objects. Its essence is revealed as true and everlasting, and it is not bound by words. The mind-nature is undefiled and perfect from the very beginning; only let go of deluded thoughts, and you are the Tathāgata as such.”

When the practice has reached this point, the method of Buddha-recitation comes into its own, and the way of response is opened between you and the Buddha; this is the very time to apply your strength.

“Its marks are like clouds dispersing from the vast sky, with the blue heavens utterly revealed, and one sees one’s original face directly. Yet in truth there is nothing seen: the unseen is the true seeing, while any seeing at all follows after dust. When you reach this, the hues of the mountains and the sound of the streams are all the ultimate truth; the cawing of crows and the chatter of magpies are none other than the supreme vehicle. Lively and vital, it responds to all dharmas without dwelling on any one of them; bright and luminous, it illumines all objects while being utterly empty of anything at all.
As for its function: it is like the morning sun rising in the east, perfectly bright and illuminating all.

As for its essence: it is like the bright moon setting in the west, pure and still, utterly quiescent. It is illuminating and yet quiescent, quiescent and yet illuminating. Both are preserved and both are dissolved, absolute and perfectly interfused. It may be likened to snow covering a thousand mountains, or the ocean swallowing ten thousand forms: there is only one color, with no other flavor at all, wholly free and unimpeded, utterly at ease.

As for its benefits: in the present, one has not yet left the Sahā world and yet already joins the assembly of the ocean-wide congregation; at the end of life, one ascends at once to the highest grade and instantly realizes the Buddha-vehicle.
Only those within the family know the family’s affairs; tell them to an outsider, and slander is certain.
He asked again: “In one’s daily life one must respond to every kind of circumstance. How can one meet bodhi in everything one sees, so that wherever one turns, all is the Way?”

Answer: “When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all dharmas cease. The ten thousand objects do not go beyond the one mind, and the one mind interpenetrates the ten thousand objects. If you understand that the essence of mind is originally empty, what hindrance is there in embracing all phenomena? Know that all phenomena are like illusions, and that arising and ceasing are nothing but the one mind. All circumstances bind you not; you are originally liberated. The six sense-objects are not evil; they are none other than perfect enlightenment. Mind and objects are one suchness—what obstruction could there be?”

“Do you not see the Avatamsaka’s dharma-realm of mutual non-obstruction in all things? It is said that within each and every mote of dust are all lands, and within each and every mind are all minds; each mind and each mote of dust again encompass one another, layer upon layer without end and without obstruction. Therefore the vessel-world, a hair, a speck of dust, the jeweled nets of cloud-terraces—all proclaim the ocean of the nature, all expound the true vehicle. Vertically they exhaust the three periods of time; horizontally they pervade the ten directions. Search for even a hair-tip’s worth that is not the Way, and you will not find it. Thus every dharma and every direction is nothing but the great field of quiescence; every mind and every thought accords with the ocean of sarvajñā—the Buddha’s all-encompassing wisdom. Only mind, wondrous object; only object, wondrous mind. Free of the four propositions and cut off from the hundred negations, absolute and perfectly interfused—how could it ever be conceived or discussed!”

What I have said above is like a blind man groping at an elephant: though I have not departed from the elephant, I fear it is not the whole elephant. I write it down to submit it to those who have seen it for themselves.

inline.s: [Master Yinguang] (

) A great monk of the late Qing and early Republican period, and the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school. He was a native of Heyang in Shaanxi; his secular surname was Zhao, his given name Shengliang, his style name Yinguang, and his alternate name the Monk of Constant Shame. He first devoted himself to Confucian learning and made it his business to refute Buddhism, but later awoke through illness and entered the Buddhist fold. In the seventh year of the Guangxu reign (

) he left home under Master Daochun at the Lotus Cave on Mount Nanwutai in the Zhongnan Mountains, and later received full ordination at Shuangxi Temple in Xing’an. From the twelfth year of Guangxu he devoted himself to the Pure Land practice at Zifu Temple on Mount Hongluo in Huairou, Beijing, and soon after moved to Yuanguang Temple in Beijing. At that time Master Huawen, abbot of Fayu Temple on Mount Putuo in Zhejiang, came to the capital seeking the Buddhist canon and invited him south; so in the nineteenth year of Guangxu he went to Fayu Temple for the summer retreat, where he read the great canon in the sutra library and delved deeply into Buddhism.

The layman Gao Henian came to Mount Putuo and carried several of his manuscripts to Shanghai, where they were published in the Buddhist Study Miscellany under the name the Monk of Constant Shame; from that time the world came to know his name.
In Nanjing he joined others in founding a place of practice for releasing life and Buddha-recitation, and established a Buddhist orphanage.
He stayed temporarily at Taiping Temple in Shanghai in order to print Zhou Mengyan’s Complete Works of Anshi.
In

of that year he moved to Baoguo Temple in Suzhou, where he shut himself away to write and completed the compilation of the gazetteers of the four great sacred mountains—Mount Putuo, Mount Wutai, Mount Emei, and Mount Jiuhua. Later he went to Lingyan Mountain Temple, where he established a place devoted exclusively to the Pure Land practice, and founded the Honghua Society in Shanghai to circulate Buddhist texts.

After the War of Resistance against Japan broke out, he took refuge at Lingyan Temple and shut his door to devote himself to Buddha-recitation. After Suzhou fell, he refused still more firmly to have dealings with the world, preserving his national integrity. Throughout his life the Master propagated the Pure Land, always showing people the path of honest and steadfast practice. His learning and his conduct were both excellent, and his lay disciples were found throughout China and abroad; he was hailed as the foremost Pure Land elder since the founding of the Republic. After his death he was honored as the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school in China. His works include A Treatise Resolving Doubts about the Pure Land, A Treatise on How the Schools and the Teachings Should Not Be Confused, and the main and supplementary editions of Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, as well as A Record of Excellent Words.
The title of this essay:
[Record of Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation-Samādhi]

[Buddha-recitation-samādhi] “Samādhi” is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term; its meaning is rendered as “concentration.” Since the concentration arises from Buddha-recitation, it is called Buddha-recitation-samādhi. [Groping the elephant] The story of the blind men groping the elephant comes from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, scroll thirty-two, and means mistaking a part for the whole. The sutra says:
(Each of the blind men touched the elephant with his hand)

He who touched the tusks said the elephant was shaped like a radish root; he who touched the ear said it was like a winnowing basket; he who touched the head said it was like a stone; he who touched the trunk said it was like a pestle; he who touched a foot said it was like a wooden mortar; he who touched the back said it was like a bed; he who touched the belly said it was like a jar; he who touched the tail said it was like a rope.”

[Record of groping the elephant] The essay is titled “Record of Groping the Elephant,” on the one hand out of the author’s modesty, and on the other hand to make plain that what it says is not a matter of mere assumption. Therefore at the end of the essay he says:

“What I have said above is like a blind man groping at an elephant. Though I have not departed from the elephant, I fear it is not the whole elephant. I write it down to submit it to those who have seen it for themselves
(to have it verified by those wise ones who have personally witnessed the state of Buddha-recitation-samādhi)
[Record] This piece is a narrative account, and so it takes “record” as its title.
Master Yinguang’s prefatory note before the text:
[Master Liaoyu’s original manuscript, lightly revised; because a few sentences were misprinted in the Buddhist Study Miscellany, the original text is recorded here.]

This is Master Liaoyu’s original manuscript, to which I have made slight revisions. Because a few sentences were misprinted when the Buddhist Study Miscellany set the type and picked out the characters, what is recorded in Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings is the original text as I wrote it.
Here Master Yinguang explains why the text recorded in the Collected Writings differs from that in the Buddhist Study Miscellany.

[Master Liaoyu] Master Liaoyu was named Guangdao and was a native of Zhejiang; he was tonsured and left home in the fourteenth year of the Guangxu reign of the Qing. Long sustained by Master Yinguang’s care, he drank deeply of the dharma-milk, and yet the two always regarded each other as fellow cultivators of the Pure Land. In the thirty-second year of Guangxu (
at the age of

) he entered retreat at Baoqing Temple in Cixi, Zhejiang, cutting off all worldly ties and affairs and cultivating the Pure Land practice, and it was then that he wrote the Record of Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation-Samādhi. In the fourth year of the Republic he served as abbot of Puji Temple, and in the ninth year of the Republic he once more retired into seclusion to cultivate the Pure Land. On New Year’s Day of the thirteenth year of the Republic (

) he said to the layman Zheng Xuetang, who had come to attend him in his illness: “There is no need. Tomorrow I shall pass away!” And indeed he was reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss the next day, at the age of sixty-one. Knowing beforehand the time of his passing, the Master rejoiced exceedingly. He established a Buddhist normal school in Nanjing and served as its principal, and his contribution to the propagation of Tiantai doctrine was outstanding. [Kuang Heng bores through the wall] Kuang Heng’s family was poor when he was young, so he bored a hole through the wall to read by his neighbor’s lamplight, and in the end became a great scholar.

After hearing Master Dixian expound the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra, I found Buddha-recitation ever more intimate: once the Buddha’s name was raised, deluded thoughts vanished completely. Truly there is nothing to compare with the bliss of Buddha-recitation!
Here the author describes the state of his own Buddha-recitation at this time.
[Sweet dew] In Sanskrit, amṛta, translated as “sweet dew.” Its taste is sweet as honey, and it is the food of the gods. The Words and Phrases on the Sutra of Immeasurable Light says:
“Sweet dew is the deathless medicine of the heavens; those who eat it live long, their bodies are at peace, their strength is great, and their bodies shine.”

Here sweet dew stands for the water of wisdom. [Sprinkling the crown] “Sprinkling” means the protection of great compassion; “crown” means the supreme fruit of Buddhahood. It means that the buddhas sprinkle the crown with the water of wisdom, enabling the merits and virtues to be perfected. [Ghee] Butter refined through repeated churning, the foremost of flavors, standing for the supreme Buddha-dharma.

One day a visitor came before the retreat cell to seek instruction and said: “I have practiced the method of Buddha-recitation for more than twenty years. In giving rise to faith, making vows, and undertaking the practice, I have not been insincere; yet my karma is deep and my hindrances heavy, and I have never reached the state of single-mindedness. Judging my own faculties, I am fit only for attaining rebirth while still carrying my karma. Though Buddha-recitation-samādhi is not something I dare hope for in this life, my heart is truly unwilling to let it go—at the very least I ought to know its method and its states. I respectfully beg the Master to expound them for me.

[Faculties] One’s basic capacity. [The method by which it may be attained] The method by which Buddha-recitation-samādhi can be realized. [The marks by which its attainment is known] The states of one who has realized Buddha-recitation-samādhi. [Attaining rebirth while carrying one’s karma] In the 1980s a doctrinal dispute arose in Buddhist circles in Taiwan and Hong Kong over “whether one who carries karma can be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.” Some held that one who carries karma can be reborn there, some that one who carries karma cannot, and some that only one who carries pure karma can. Opinion was divided, and to this day there is no settled conclusion. In fact, as far as putting an end to birth and death and escaping the three realms is concerned, the excellence of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss lies in the fact that one need not cut off the delusions of views and thoughts in order to put an end to birth and death, whereas the ordinary paths must cut them off before birth and death can be ended. Therefore the accurate formulation should be “attaining rebirth while carrying delusion” (where “delusion” means the delusions of views and thoughts). [The delusions of views and thoughts] The delusion of views and the delusion of thoughts. The delusion of views is the ordinary person’s confusion and error in understanding, such as the five false views of the view of a self, extreme views, false views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions; the delusion of thoughts is the ordinary person’s confusion and error in thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of beings’ drifting through the three realms and suffering birth and death to no purpose; cut them off, and one can put an end to birth and death and escape the three realms.

[I replied: “The states and marks of samādhi are known only to one who has realized them, as when a person drinks water and alone knows for himself whether it is cold or warm. Since I have not realized it, how could I expound it?” The visitor pleaded again and again without cease.]

I answered: “The states and marks of Buddha-recitation-samādhi are known only to one who has realized them, as when a person drinks water and alone knows for himself whether it is cold or warm. Since I have not realized Buddha-recitation-samādhi, how could I expound it to you?” The visitor pleaded again and again without cease.

In what follows, the author answers the visitor’s questions about the method and the states of Buddha-recitation-samādhi, setting forth its method of cultivation, its state of realization, and its marks, function, essence, and benefits.

blocks.text: 2. Turning the Recitation Back into Contemplation

inline.s: Reciting the name of the Buddha may be done as practice at the level of phenomena or as practice at the level of principle. Practice at the level of phenomena is to recite Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice at the level of principle is to recite the Buddha of one’s own nature (the Amitābha of self-nature). Practice at the level of phenomena is urgently directed toward rebirth; practice at the level of principle aims at seeing the nature. Master Hanshan records in his Stele Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi:
“Question: Can one awaken
(see the nature)
through Buddha-recitation? The Master
(Master Lianchi)
said: ‘Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.’ Why then doubt that turning the recitation back to recite the self-nature does the same?”

(Translation: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says, “Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.” Why should one doubt that turning the recitation back to recite the self-nature can likewise accomplish the supreme Way? The meaning of this passage is: turning the recitation back to recite the self-nature likewise accomplishes the supreme Way.)
Master Yinguang said:
“Turn the recitation back to recite the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.”
(Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, volume four, Second Letter in Reply to the Layman Qi Zhizhou)
[Turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature]
Turn your false hearing, which follows sound outward, back around, and hear the self-nature within.

[The nature accomplishes the supreme Way] (Through turning the hearing back to the self-nature) the self-nature is transformed from the state of consciousness into the state of original nature (returning to the source), and one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood (the supreme Way).
[The supreme Way] The Way attained by the Tathāgata, beyond which there is nothing higher; hence it is called the supreme Way. The Lotus Sūtra,
Chapter on Skilful Means, says:
“Uprightly setting aside skilful means, they proclaim only the supreme Way.”
The Lotus Sūtra,
Chapter on the Length of Life, says:
“Each constantly forms this thought: by what means may beings enter the supreme Way and quickly accomplish the Buddha-body?”

Practice at the level of principle must be undertaken on the foundation of having already attained single-mindedness through practice at the level of phenomena; only then can one avoid the disaster of falling into emptiness. Master Yinguang said:

“Because of the Amitābha of self-nature, one must recite the Amitābha of the West in order to seek rebirth, and by advancing gradually one may personally realize the Amitābha of self-nature. If one clings solely to the Amitābha of self-nature and does not recite the Amitābha of the West, then even if one truly awakens
(sees the nature)
, one still cannot at once put an end to birth and death.”
(Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings
Twenty-Seven Answers to Questions from the Layman Qu Tianxiang)

To cultivate Buddha-recitation-samādhi is practice at the level of principle: reciting the Buddha of self-nature (the Amitābha of self-nature) in order to see through to the original face. Master Lianchi said:

“Know that the Pure Land is only mind, and there is no outer realm at all.” “When one accords with principle, the self-nature returns to its own essence—this is the meaning of vowing to be born in that land.” “To recite the Buddha is to recite the mind; being born there does not depart from being born here. Mind, Buddha, and beings are one substance, and one does not dwell on either bank of the midstream. Hence it is called the Amitābha of self-nature and the Pure Land of mind-only.”
(Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra)

[Mind, Buddha, and beings are one substance] Buddha and beings are two states of the mind: when the mind awakens it is Buddha, when the mind is deluded it is a being. [One does not dwell on either bank of the midstream] Master Lianchi explains in his Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra:

“As for the two banks of the midstream: Sahā stands for this side and Sukhāvatī for that. At first one rejects suffering and delights in bliss; then suffering and bliss both vanish; finally one does not dwell even in the neither-suffering-nor-bliss. This is what is meant by not clinging to the two extremes and not resting in the middle way.”
[Not resting in the middle way] Not dwelling in the neither-suffering-nor-bliss.
Concerning practice at the level of phenomena and practice at the level of principle, Master Lianchi taught:

“Uninterrupted recollection is called practice at the level of phenomena; uninterrupted investigation is called practice at the level of principle. This will be discussed in detail below, and this is taken as the cause. The single-mindedness spoken of later also has its phenomenal and its principled aspect. Those who do not understand this think that Buddha-recitation is for the dull faculties, and that only Chan meditation can awaken to the Way. Beginners, hearing this, cannot decide for themselves. They do not know that investigating Buddha-recitation is very close in meaning to what the venerable ones of former generations taught when they told people to raise a meditative topic and give rise to doubt. Hence it is said that in Chan one need not raise a separate topic, but need only settle upon the single phrase Amitābha Buddha. How wonderful a saying!”
(Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra)

[The single-mindedness spoken of later also has its phenomenal and its principled aspect.] The single-mindedness discussed later also includes single-mindedness in phenomena and single-mindedness in principle. Master Ouyi said:

“Single-mindedness in phenomena means being perfectly clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered; single-mindedness in principle means silently according with the unborn and clearly understanding the self-nature.”

(Collected Essays from Lingfeng, Casual Talks from the Brahma Chamber) [The unborn] Without arising or ceasing (since it is originally unborn, it is also unceasing); that is, the principle of nirvāṇa. The Sūtra of the Supreme King says:
“The unborn is real; birth is false. The foolish drift and drown in birth and death; the Tathāgata embodies the real, without any falseness, and this is called nirvāṇa.”
[Thinking that Buddha-recitation is for the dull faculties] Thinking that Buddha-recitation applies only to people of dull faculties.
Concerning single-mindedness in phenomena and single-mindedness in principle, Master Lianchi continued:
(Reciting the name of the Buddha)

is divided into the phenomenal and the principled: uninterrupted recollection is called practice at the level of phenomena; uninterrupted investigation is called practice at the level of principle. As for recollection: hearing the Buddha’s name, one constantly remembers and constantly recites it, taking it as the object of the mind, so that every word is clear and distinct, and phrase follows phrase in unbroken succession. Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is only this one thought and no second thought, and one is not disordered by thoughts of greed, anger, or any other affliction. This is what the Sūtra on Accomplishing the Light of Meditative Intent means when it says: ‘In leisure and solitude, one single-minds the mind; amid all afflictions, one single-minds the mind; even amid praise and blame, gain and loss, good and evil, one single-minds the mind in every case.’ One attains it on the phenomenal level but has not penetrated it on the principled level, having only obtained the power of faith and not yet seen the Way; this is called single-mindedness in phenomena.

“As for investigation: hearing the Buddha’s name, one does not merely recollect it, but turns the recitation back into contemplation, observing and examining it, interrogating its root. When investigation reaches its utmost, one suddenly accords with one’s own original mind. Within this there are again two aspects. First, the non-duality of suchness and wisdom. Outside the reciting mind there is no Buddha for me to recite—this is wisdom without suchness; outside the recited Buddha there is no mind that can recite the Buddha—this is suchness without wisdom. Neither suchness nor wisdom, and so there is only the one mind. Second, the inconceivability of stillness and illumination. If you say it exists, then the essence of the reciting mind is empty of itself, and the recited Buddha is utterly ungraspable. If you say it does not exist, then the reciting mind is spiritually aware and not obscured, and the recited Buddha is perfectly clear and distinct. If you say it both exists and does not exist, then both the reciting and the non-reciting are dissolved. If you say it neither exists nor does not exist, then both the reciting and the non-reciting are preserved. Since it is not existent, it is ever still; since it is not nonexistent, it is ever illuminating; since it is neither both nor neither, it is neither still nor illuminating, and yet illuminating and still. The path of words and thought is cut off, and it cannot be described; hence there is only the one mind. Here the feelings of the grasped and the grasper melt away and the views of existence and nonexistence are exhausted, and in the pure and originally natural essence, what dharma could there be to disorder it? Because one has seen the truth, this is called single-mindedness in principle. Indeed, phenomena arise relying on principle, and principle is made manifest through phenomena; phenomena and principle mutually support each other and neither may be abandoned. Yet if one fixes on phenomena and one’s recitation can continue in succession, one does not waste the merit of entering the grades; while if one clings to principle and the mind is in fact not yet clear, one instead suffers the disaster of falling into emptiness.”
(The Yunqi Dharma Collection)

[Interrogate (jú)] To probe to the bottom. [Suchness and wisdom] “Suchness” is the dharmakāya Buddha that is recited (the Amitābha of self-nature), and “wisdom” is the mind that recites. [Mutually support] To depend on and make manifest each other. [Seeing the truth] To see the truth. In the śrāvaka vehicle one must be at least a stream-enterer to see the truth; bodhisattvas must be at least on the first ground to see the truth.

Concerning practice at the level of principle, Master Lianchi warned that “if one clings to principle and the mind is in fact not yet clear, one instead suffers the disaster of falling into emptiness.” The safe road, therefore, is this: first attain single-mindedness through practice at the level of phenomena, so that rebirth is assured, and then, on that foundation, take up practice at the level of principle in order to clarify the mind and see the nature. In this way one will not only avoid “the disaster of falling into emptiness,” but having attained single-mindedness in phenomena and then taking up practice at the level of principle, the path of principle will be clear and the practice will have power.
Question: How can one attain single-mindedness in phenomena?
Answer: The greatest obstacle to attaining single-mindedness in phenomena is deluded thoughts. In the practical-training textbook of the “Buddhist College Online, Practice as Taught” series,
Mindful Buddha-Recitation

, the causes of deluded thoughts are analyzed in detail, together with how to overcome them effectively; and the specific steps and methods for attaining single-mindedness in phenomena are explained in detail. If one has true faith and earnest vows, works hard, proceeds step by step, and perseveres, one will certainly attain single-mindedness in phenomena.

[I replied: As for the method itself, one must, at the very moment of reciting, turn the recitation back into contemplation, focusing intently upon a single object and never letting the mind wander outward; thought after thought tends the source of mind, mind after mind accords with the Buddha-essence.]

So I said: As for the method of Buddha-recitation-samādhi, one must, at the moment of reciting, turn the recitation back into contemplation of the self-nature (reciting inward, looking inward). One must focus intently upon a single object and never let the mind wander outward; thought after thought tends the mind itself (the source of mind), and mind after mind accords with the self-nature (the Buddha-essence).

Thought after thought”: every thought of reciting the Buddha. “Thought after thought tends the mind itself; mind after mind accords with the self-nature”—this is turning the recitation back to recite the self-nature (reciting the Buddha of self-nature): sound after sound awakening the master within. Master Lianchi said:

“In Buddha-recitation...... each phrase must leave the mouth and enter the ear, and sound after sound awakens one’s own mind. It is like one person deep asleep and another calling out, ‘So-and-so!’ and that person wakes at once. This is why Buddha-recitation is the best means of gathering in the mind.”
(The Posthumous Manuscripts of Master Yunqi)
[The source of mind] The mind is the root source of all dharmas, and so it is called the source of mind. A Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:

“If deluded thoughts arise, know them and do not follow them. When delusion ceases, the source of mind is empty and still. The ten thousand virtues are complete within it, and its wondrous function is inexhaustible.”
Great Calming and Contemplation says:
“Cross-legged, with hands folded, lips closed and tongue still, contemplate the ultimate reality; the source of mind is stilled in one, and the whole dharma-realm is likewise quiescent.”
It also says:
“If you wish to illumine and know, you must know the source of mind. When the source of mind is non-dual, all dharmas are alike as empty space.”
[The Buddha-essence] The self-nature.
Beings are deluded as to their self-nature and falsely take the body and mind of the five aggregates as a self; hence they turn about in birth and death. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“From beginningless time all beings have had all kinds of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another
(who cannot tell east from west, south from north)

, falsely taking the four great elements as the marks of their own body and the shadows cast by the six sense-objects as the marks of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! In the sky there are truly no flowers; the sick person falsely grasps at them. Because of this false grasping, he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this space, but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. Hence there falsely exists the turning about in birth and death, and this is called ignorance.”
Turning the recitation back to recite the self-nature is precisely to shatter this beginningless ignorance.

[The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five arise from accumulation, and so they are called the “five aggregates”; they can also cover over a person’s true nature, causing confusion and inversion and the creation of all kinds of karma, and so they are also called the “five shadows.” Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called the “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called the “dharmas of mind.” These are the five great constituents of body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form is the body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness) are the mind. [The four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture, fire has warmth, and wind has motion. All the material things of the world possess these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion, and so they are called “great.” [The shadows cast by the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced when the six faculties come into contact with the six sense-objects; and because these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows cast by the six sense-objects—the phantom shadows cast by contact with the six sense-objects. The verse of Vipaśyī Buddha says:

“Borrowing the four great elements, one takes them as a body; the mind is originally unborn and exists because of objects. If the objects before it were absent, the mind too would be absent; guilt and merit, like illusions, arise and cease as well.”
(The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
Question: The self-nature has no shape or mark—how is one to contemplate it?
Answer: The Chan Master Linji said:
“On this lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, who comes in and out through the gates of your faces. Those who have not yet witnessed it—look!”
(The Record of Linji) The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.”
The method of this essay is:
Turn the recitation back to recite the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.
Master Lianchi’s Yunqi Dharma Collection says:

“As for investigation: hearing the Buddha’s name, one does not merely recollect it, but turns the recitation back into contemplation, observing and examining it, interrogating its root. When investigation reaches its utmost, one suddenly accords with one’s own original mind.”
Master Hanshan
’s Record of Dream Wanderings, Stele Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi, records:
“The imperial censor Zuo Zongying asked: Can one awaken through Buddha-recitation? The Master
(Master Lianchi)
said: ‘Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way. Why then doubt turning the recitation back to recite the self-nature?’”

[The recitation returns to the recitation itself, the contemplation returns to the contemplation itself; the reciting is the contemplating, and the contemplating is the reciting. One must bring it about that the whole of the recitation is contemplation, with no contemplation apart from the recitation; and the whole of the contemplation is recitation, with no recitation apart from the contemplation.]

Turning the recitation back to the self-nature, the self-nature is in the recitation; turning the contemplation back to the self-nature, the self-nature is in the contemplation; reciting while contemplating, contemplating while reciting. One must make every moment of recitation a moment of contemplation (the whole of the recitation is contemplation, with no contemplation apart from the recitation), and every moment of contemplation a moment of recitation (the whole of the contemplation is recitation, with no recitation apart from the contemplation), so that contemplation and recitation completely coincide.
The Chan Master Zhongfeng’s Liturgical Model for the Three Sessions of Recitation says:
“Recite it long, and outside the recitation there is no other Buddha, and outside the Buddha no other recitation.”
It also says:
“Thus one knows that the assembly now present, by means of the Amitābha of self-nature and the tongue-roots of the great assembly together, universally turns the fundamental dharma-wheel.”
This is precisely the first stage of what Master Lianchi above called practice at the level of principle, “the non-duality of suchness and wisdom”:

“Outside the reciting mind there is no Buddha for me to recite—this is wisdom without suchness; outside the recited Buddha there is no mind that can recite the Buddha—this is suchness without wisdom. Neither suchness nor wisdom, and so there is only the one mind.”
Master Lianchi’s Yunqi Dharma Collection says:

“As for investigation: hearing the Buddha’s name, one does not merely recollect it, but turns the recitation back into contemplation, examining it to the utmost, interrogating its root. When investigation reaches its utmost, one suddenly accords with one’s own original mind.”
Master Hanshan’s Record of Dream Wanderings,
Essential Pointers for Chan Investigation, says:

“The tongs and hammers that old man Dahui habitually used were meant only to block off the flow of deluded thinking beneath the faculty of intellect at the meditative topic, so that it could not proceed; and right where it cannot proceed, to look upon one’s original face.”
[Though contemplation and recitation are already blended like water and milk, the root has not yet been interrogated to the bottom.

Though contemplation and recitation have already become one piece (no contemplation apart from the recitation, no recitation apart from the contemplation), the root has not yet been probed to the bottom (one has not yet seen the original face).
[Interrogating to the root] Probing to the very root. “Interrogate
(jú)
,” pronounced like “ju,” means to probe to the bottom; “root” means the original face (the original nature).
The state in which “

contemplation and recitation are already blended like water and milk” is “like clarifying muddy water: the sand and earth settle of themselves, and clear water appears before one; this is called the initial subduing of the dust of affliction.” One must still interrogate it to the root before it is “removing the mud and having pure water, which is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance.” The next step, therefore, is to interrogate it to the root by investigating again and again (to see the original face directly).
Master Hanshan said:

“If one is amid the defilement and turbidity of affliction, a single utterance of the Buddha’s name is like a water-clearing pearl; one may enjoy its benefit thereby, but it is not yet a thorough probing to the source. The sutra says: like clarifying muddy water, the sand and earth settle of themselves, and clear water appears before one; this is called the initial subduing of the dust of affliction. Removing the mud and having pure water is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance.”
(Record of Dream Wanderings,
Instructions to Liu Cunchi)
[The water-clearing pearl] Zhongfeng’s Three Sessions of Recitation says:

“The ancients said: cast a clear pearl into turbid water, and the turbid water cannot but become clear; cast Buddha-recitation into a scattered mind, and the scattered mind cannot but become Buddha. In the West there is a jewel called the clear pearl. It is said that when this pearl is cast into turbid water, for every inch it sinks the turbid water for that inch becomes clean at once. As the pearl sinks from an inch to a foot and so down to the bottom, the turbid water clears along with it. Know that the clear pearl stands for the pure thought of Buddha-recitation, and the turbid water for the scattered and deluded mind.”
[You must take that single
(here meaning “this”)
thought of ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’ and investigate it again and again, rousing yourself to it with all earnestness.]
You must take this single thought of ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’ and, closely and ever more deeply, investigate (accord with) the self-nature, earnestly and vigilantly preserving right mindfulness.
[Rousing to it] Vigilantly preserving right mindfulness. Master Lianchi said:
“I beg you to let go of the ten thousand conditions and, throughout the twelve hours
(twenty-four hours)
of the day, rouse yourself to it thought after thought. This is my utmost hope.”
(Yunqi Dharma Collection) The Gateless Gate of the Chan School says:
“With the three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores of your whole body, raise a mass of doubt and investigate the word ‘none,’ rousing yourself to it day and night.”
Master Zhu’s Complete Works, ·Preserving and Nourishing, says:
“One need only constantly rouse oneself to it, accumulating little by little; in time it will naturally continue without interruption and become one piece.”

The monk Ruiyan used to ask himself every day: “Master, are you clear?” And he would answer himself: “Clear.” [Clear] Lucid and alert. For a practitioner, falling into deluded thoughts or into torpor is a failure of lucidity, because one is not one’s own master.

The method is this: raise one utterance of the Buddha’s name, and at once accord inwardly with the self-nature—; raise one utterance of the Buddha’s name, and at once accord inwardly with the self-nature—;

and so continue, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. First one must reach the point where, apart from the Buddha’s name, there is no second thought. As the practice deepens, one gradually lengthens the interval between two utterances of the Buddha’s name, still keeping to the point where, apart from the Buddha’s name, there is no second thought. When that interval has already become very long and still no second thought arises, one no longer raises the Buddha’s name (to raise it again would be “adding a head on top of a head”), but simply accords inwardly with the self-nature. As days pass and the practice deepens, without according it accords of itself, utterly one piece. When the time and conditions come and one is touched or bumped, suddenly there is a great awakening (seeing the nature through and through).

The essential points in doing the work of investigation are these: to make the accord with the nature focused, continuous, and lasting. Moreover, one must keep a firm guard over deluded thoughts: not letting a single thought slip past (not being deceived by it), and seeing through every thought (not being shrouded by it, not following its tricks, not taking it as real). Whenever a deluded thought arises, it shows that the accord with the self-nature has been interrupted, or that one has even forgotten to accord with the self-nature. One must at once rouse one’s spirits and, with still greater focus and continuity, accord with the self-nature; the deluded thoughts will then cease of themselves. If instead one loathes the deluded thought and wants to drive it out and destroy it, one is placing one’s attention on the deluded thought, which only makes it more solid and more fierce.
Therefore, when deluded thoughts circle about and will not leave, use the accord with the self-nature to break them up and melt them away; this is prajñā perfuming ignorance.
One may also do this:
raise one utterance of the Buddha’s name,
then turn the hearing back to the self-nature

, making this turning back of the hearing close and unbroken; if it is broken, raise the name again, and if it is not broken, do not raise it—the fewer times it is raised, the better. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must take good care of the practice and not let it be lost. When one does not raise the Buddha’s name and merely turns the hearing back without any deluded thought, then one stops raising it altogether,
and simply
turns the hearing back to the self-nature.

As days pass and the practice deepens, without hearing one hears of itself, utterly one piece. When the time and conditions come and one is touched or bumped, suddenly there is a great awakening (seeing the nature through and through).
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra,
Chapter on Perfect Penetration through the Ear-Faculty, says:
“Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature, and the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.”
(Please refer to
Awareness of Chan
, the chapter on “Perfect Penetration through the Ear-Faculty.”)
[Turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature]
Turn your false hearing, which follows sound outward, back around, and hear the self-nature within.

[The nature accomplishes the supreme Way] (Through turning the hearing back to the self-nature) the self-nature is transformed from the state of consciousness into the state of original nature (returning to the source), and one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood (the supreme Way).
[The supreme Way] The Way attained by the Tathāgata, beyond which there is nothing higher; hence it is called the supreme Way.
The Lotus Sūtra says:
“Each constantly forms this thought: by what means may beings enter the supreme Way and quickly accomplish the Buddha-body?”
Question: How does one accord with the self-nature?
Answer: The self-nature is the inner spiritual energy (see
Mind, Self-Nature, Tathāgatagarbha

for details). To accord with the self-nature is to be aware of it, to feel it, and to become one with it. For beings, the body is the shell of the self-nature, its dwelling. The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The body of form is a house and dwelling.”
The Chan Master Linji said:
“Just look at the puppets on the stage—the pulling of the strings depends entirely on the man inside.”
This means that the body of form is like a wooden puppet, and that what manipulates this body of form is the self-nature. Hence the Formula for Cultivating the Mind says:
“When the hundred bones are scattered, they return to fire, return to wind; one thing remains ever numinous, covering heaven and covering earth.”

Throughout the twelve hours of the day, to know hunger and know thirst, to know cold and know heat, to be angry or glad—this is the self-nature. The body of form is gathered from the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is dull and insentient—how could it see, hear, feel, and know? What can see, hear, feel, and know must be your self-nature. A patriarch said:

“The four great elements do not understand how to expound the dharma or listen to the dharma, and empty space does not understand how to expound the dharma or listen to the dharma. Only that which is before your eyes, clear and luminously alone, without any shape or segment, understands how to expound the dharma and listen to the dharma. That which is called the shapeless
(that which has no form or mark)
, namely, is your self-nature.”
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“It is like a wooden man and like a reanimated corpse
(made to rise and walk and move about)
, which, through the mechanical power of the piśāca
(a kind of spirit, here the animating force)
, shakes and turns and moves without cease
(acting without stopping)

[Not departing from the self-nature—this is itself the field of merit] Not departing from the self-nature, one no longer falsely clings to the body and mind of the five aggregates as a self, but rather the master within is in charge: “Those who awaken to this and keep to it sit in one suchness and move not, liberated”—this is the greatest field of merit. Ordinarily, what people never part from, like shadow and form, is that “I” of the body and mind of the five aggregates. When you have left that “I” without departing from the self-nature, this is the state of clear awareness. Not departing from that “I” of the body and mind of the five aggregates is creating karma; but to abandon that “I” and not depart from the self-nature is to plant the field of merit and to give rise constantly to wisdom. The Formula for Cultivating the Mind says:

“Those who awaken to this and keep to it sit in one suchness and move not, liberated; those who are deluded about this and turn away from it go to the six destinies and the long kalpas of transmigration.”
The Chan Master Linji, ascending the hall, said:
“On this lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, who constantly comes in and out through the gates of your faces. Those who have not yet witnessed it—look!”
(The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source)
Yu Daopo was a woman of Jinling who made her living selling oil-fried cakes
(a kind of fried glutinous-rice food)
. She used often
(the character here means “once, formerly”)
to follow the assembly in inquiring of Langya
(the Chan Master Huijue Guangzhao of Langya Mountain in Chuzhou)
, who showed her the story of Linji
(Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou in the Tang, heir of Huangbo and founder of the Linji school)
about the true person of no rank. One day, hearing a beggar singing the Lotus Joy: ‘Had Liu Yi not carried the letter, how could he ever have reached Lake Dongting
(had she not looked into the true person of no rank, how could she ever have seen the original face)

?’ she suddenly had a great awakening and flung her cake tray to the ground. Her husband looked askance and said, ‘Are you mad?’ The old woman slapped him and said, ‘This is not your realm.’ She went to see Langya. He looked at her and knew what she had attained. He asked, ‘Which one is the true person of no rank?’ The old woman answered on the instant: ‘There is a person of no rank, with six arms and three heads, striving in anger; one blow splits Mount Hua in two, and the waters flow for ten thousand years without knowing spring.’ From this her fame spread
(in abundance)
far and wide.”
(The Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
The record of Yu Daopo is taken from the Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp.

[Had Liu Yi not carried the letter] This is an inverted sentence used to heighten the emphasis; the meaning is: Liu Yi, had he not carried the letter. [Liu Yi carries the letter] The story comes from the Tang tale “The Tale of Liu Yi”: in the second year of Yifeng of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang, Liu Yi failed the examinations and went to visit a friend in Jinghe county, where on the bank of the Jing River he saw a woman tending sheep. The shepherdess looked sorrowful, as though waiting for something. Liu Yi, puzzled, asked her, and learned that the woman was the daughter of the Dragon King of Lake Dongting and the wife of the young dragon of the Jing River. The young dragon of the Jing River was coarse and foolish, and was bewitched by his maidservants; husband and wife were at odds, and the dragon girl was punished to tend sheep on the bank of the Jing River in suffering. Hearing this, Liu Yi’s blood stirred with indignation and deep sympathy, and he accepted the dragon girl’s entreaty to carry her letter home to the dragon palace in Lake Dongting. When the dragon girl’s uncle, the Qiantang Fire Dragon, learned of it, he flew into a rage, led his water troops to the Jing River, swallowed the young dragon of the Jing River alive, and rescued the dragon girl.

“You must take that single thought of ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’ and investigate it again and again, rousing yourself to it with all earnestness.” This may also be understood as: you must take this single thought of ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’ and ever more deeply investigate it:
Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?
earnestly and vigilantly preserving right mindfulness.

The method is this: softly raise one utterance of the Buddha’s name, and then turn the light around to shine back: what is the original face (who is it that recites the Buddha’s name)? After a long while, if a deluded thought arises, raise it again in the same way and look in the same way; if no deluded thought arises, simply look on.
Master Lianchi said:

“Now, when deluded thoughts are flying in confusion, simply raise the Buddha’s name softly once and then stop, and look to see who it is that recites the Buddha? After a long while, when a thought arises
(when a deluded thought arises)
, raise it again in the same way and look in the same way; if no thought arises, simply look on.”
(Yunqi’s Collected Sayings on the Pure Land)
Master Hanshan said:
“Whenever anyone, noble or humble, monastic or lay, entered his room,
(Master Yungu)

he would throw a sitting cushion on the ground and make the person sit upright and turn back to contemplate his own original face. Sometimes a whole day and night passed without a single word. On parting he would always enjoin: ‘Do not let the day pass in vain.’ On meeting again he would always ask: ‘Since we parted, how have you found the work of the mind—difficult or easy?’”
(Record of Dream Wanderings
Biography of the Late Master Yungu)
Master Lianchi’s Yunqi’s Collected Sayings on the Pure Land says:

“Raising a meditative topic is the most urgent and essential work for awakening in the Chan school. For one who cultivates the Pure Land, taking a single utterance of the Buddha’s name as the meditative topic is a wonderful method. But if the mind is coarse and the energy flighty, one cannot be in accord with it. One must sink deep and shine back, until strength is exhausted and the situation is spent, and then there is a sudden crack of news.”
It also says:

“Birth and death do not depart from a single thought, and all dharmas, worldly and world-transcending, do not depart from a single thought. Now if one recites the Buddha with this very thought, how close and how essential it is. If one sees through where this thought arises, that is the Amitābha of self-nature, that is the patriarchs’ meaning in coming from the West. Even if one does not awaken, riding the power of this thought one will be reborn in Ultimate Bliss, and will cut birth and death crosswise, no longer subject to transmigration, and in the end will surely awaken greatly. May you, sir, let go of the ten thousand conditions and, throughout the twelve hours, rouse yourself to it thought after thought. This is my utmost hope!”

(Here Master Lianchi says: if one sees through where this thought arises, that is clarifying the mind and seeing the nature; and even if one cannot see through it, riding the power of this thought one will still be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, cutting birth and death crosswise, no longer subject to transmigration, and in the end will surely awaken greatly. Therefore investigating Buddha-recitation is an extremely safe method. May you let go of the ten thousand conditions and, throughout the twelve hours, rouse yourself to it thought after thought; this is my utmost hope!)
It also says: “

Desire is the root of birth as a human being, and to cut it off is truly difficult. There is the contemplation of impurity, which treats the symptoms; and there is investigating back into where the thought of desire arises, which treats the root. Now one need only investigate who it is that recites the Buddha.”

(Translation: Desire is the root cause of transmigration through the six destinies, and to cut it off is truly difficult. One should use the contemplation of impurity to treat the symptoms, and investigate back into where the thought of desire arises to treat the root. Now one need only investigate who it is that recites the Buddha, and both symptom and root are treated.)

One point requires special attention: the investigating of Buddha-recitation that Master Lianchi taught is the investigation of who it is that recites the Buddha. The meditative topic is the Buddha’s name, not “who recites the Buddha’s name.”
Master Lianchi said:
Raising a meditative topic is the most urgent and essential work for awakening in the Chan school. For one who cultivates the Pure Land,
taking a single utterance of the Buddha’s name as the meditative topic
is a wonderful method.”
(Yunqi’s Collected Sayings on the Pure Land)

[Taking a single utterance of the Buddha’s name as the meditative topic] There is a mistaken approach in investigating Buddha-recitation: taking “who recites the Buddha’s name” as the meditative topic, and then using the conceptual mind to think and conjecture about who it is that recites the Buddha. That is not investigation but the playing out of deluded thoughts, and it runs directly counter to clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.
The method of investigation is: look to see who it is that recites the Buddha’s name.
Master Lianchi said:
Now, when deluded thoughts are flying in confusion, simply raise the Buddha’s name softly once and then stop,
and look to see who it is that recites the Buddha.
After a long while, when a thought arises
(when after a long time a deluded thought suddenly arises)
, raise it again in the same way and look in the same way;
if no thought arises, simply look on
(Yunqi’s Collected Sayings on the Pure Land)

The “looking” spoken of here is not looking with the fleshly eye, but turning the light around to shine back upon the master within who recites the Buddha. So long as one is shining back, no deluded thought arises; and if a deluded thought does arise, it shows that the shining back has been lost. At that moment one must at once gather one’s attention again and turn the light back to shine.
The reason that one should immediately raise one utterance of the Buddha’s name (the meditative topic) whenever a deluded thought arises is that this has three functions:
1. It warns oneself to be aware and not deluded;
2. It reminds one to gather one’s attention at once and turn the light back to shine;

3. Because one already has some practice in reciting the Buddha’s name, the moment the name is raised deluded thoughts vanish completely. One thereupon escapes from the deluded thoughts, creating the conditions for turning the light back to shine without any deluded thought (the doubt-mass).
There are three stages in investigating Buddha-recitation:
1. Raise one utterance of the Buddha’s name, then
turn the light back to shine: who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? This is the state in which the ten thousand thoughts return to one.

2. As days pass and the practice deepens, suddenly there is clarity and stillness. At this point one need not raise the Buddha’s name, but simply shines back, and no deluded thought will arise either. This is the state in which the one returns to nothing.

3. The grasped and the grasper both vanish (the shining and what is shone upon are both dissolved). This is the state of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature (personally realizing the original nature).
Question: What is the doubt-mass in investigating Buddha-recitation?
Answer: The state of shining back without any deluded thought is itself the doubt-mass. One must make the doubt-mass into a stretch, into a piece, into a mass.
Question: Are investigating Buddha-recitation and contemplating Buddha-recitation one thing or two?

Answer: They are one; “contemplating Buddha-recitation” is another name for “investigating Buddha-recitation.” In his teachings Master Lianchi uses both the term “investigation” and the term “contemplation.” For example:
In the Yunqi Dharma Collection Master Lianchi says:
“Now ‘one who recites the Buddha simply
investigates
while reciting the Buddha’s name’ is still one gate, not two matters. If
investigation
is not convenient, then simply reciting straight on will also do.”
It also says:
“Question: In Chan meditation what matters is that not a single thought arises, while in Buddha-recitation what matters is that pure thoughts continue in succession. This gate of
investigating Buddha-recitation
is meant for wondrous awakening and, through it, rebirth.”
It also says:

Truly, if one sees through where this single thought of Buddha-recitation arises, you may be sure the great matter is finished. Yet one must not, on seeing this said, set to thinking and conjecturing, forcing an interpretation in order to understand it; for then one loses it instead. Simply
contemplate
it thought after thought, truly accumulating strength over time until you come by it yourself—only that is realization and awakening.

(Translation: Truly, if one sees through where this single thought of Buddha-recitation arises, you may be sure the great matter of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature is finished. Yet one must not, on seeing me say “if one sees through where this single thought of Buddha-recitation arises, you may be sure the great matter is finished,” go on to think about and conjecture the meaning of these words, forcing an interpretation in order to understand it. If one does so, one loses the true purport instead. Simply, with whole-hearted singleness, contemplate and examine it within the state of no-thought; when one truly applies effort and accumulates strength in this way, one will come by it oneself in time, and only this is realization and awakening.)
[Thinking and conjecturing (
bǔ
)] To think about and conjecture. [Forcing an interpretation in order to understand it] To strain for an interpretation in order to achieve understanding.
It also says:
As for contemplation

: hearing the Buddha’s name, one does not merely recollect it, but turns the recitation back into contemplation, examining it to the utmost and interrogating its root. When contemplation reaches its utmost, one suddenly accords with one’s own original mind.”
It also says:

“Suffering arises from the body, the body arises from karma, and so on. Illness is one form of suffering, and its causal chain, each link producing the next, is likewise so. One should diligently and closely, day and night,
contemplate

it. If contemplation does not succeed, one need only raise one utterance of the fundamental meditative topic of Buddha-recitation and turn the light back to look at oneself. If one recognizes where this thought comes to rest, delusion breaks of itself. When delusion is broken, it is in turn extinguished link by link, and likewise so.”

(Translation: Suffering arises from the body, the body from karma, karma from delusion, and so on. Illness is one form of suffering, and so it too is delusion, karma, body, and suffering, each producing the next in turn. One should diligently and closely contemplate it day and night. If contemplation does not succeed, one need only raise one utterance of the fundamental meditative topic of Buddha-recitation (the Buddha’s name) and turn the light back to shine: who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? If one recognizes where this thought comes to rest, delusion breaks of itself. When delusion is broken, karma is broken; when karma is broken, the body is broken; when the body is broken, suffering (illness) is broken—and so each is extinguished in turn.)
In the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra Master Lianchi says:
“Uninterrupted recollection is called practice at the level of phenomena;
uninterrupted contemplation

is called practice at the level of principle. This will be discussed in detail below, and this is taken as the cause. The single-mindedness spoken of later also has its phenomenal and its principled aspect. Those who do not understand this think that Buddha-recitation is for the dull faculties, and that only Chan meditation can awaken to the Way. Beginners, hearing this, cannot decide for themselves. They do not know that
investigating Buddha-recitation

is very close in meaning to what the venerable ones of former generations taught when they told people to raise a meditative topic and give rise to doubt. Hence it is said that in Chan one need not raise a separate topic, but need only settle upon the single phrase Amitābha Buddha. How wonderful a saying!”
In the Second Bundle from the Bamboo Window Master Lianchi devotes a chapter to “
investigating Buddha-recitation
, in which he says:
In our dynasty
the Ming
, between the Hongwu and Yongle reigns
the reigns of Hongwu and Yongle

, there were the three elders Konggu, Tianqi, and Dufeng. In their discussions of Buddha-recitation, both Masters Tianqi and Dufeng taught people to look into “who recites the Buddha’s name”; only Konggu held that simply reciting straight on also affords a gate to awakening.
Question: Are investigating Buddha-recitation and Chan meditation the same thing?

Answer: They are alike in some ways and different in others. In what they share, both bring effort to bear where no thought has yet stirred, in order to smash the old pit of ignorance. In what differs, one who investigates Buddha-recitation has faith and vows in full, and always keeps the Buddha’s name stored in the heart; so even if the old pit of ignorance is not smashed, riding the power of this thought one will still be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, cutting birth and death crosswise. The latter practice, by contrast, must cut off the delusions of views and thoughts completely before birth and death can be ended. Therefore the former is the safer way to practice.

[The old pit of ignorance] Also called the black lacquer bucket; that is, fundamental ignorance (beginningless ignorance). [Fundamental ignorance] Also called beginningless ignorance: from beginningless time the self-nature, in a single moment of non-awakening, has been lost in the long night of confusion, not understanding the truth, and able to produce all delusions and afflictions. [The delusions of views and thoughts] The delusion of views and the delusion of thoughts. The delusion of views is the ordinary person’s confusion and error in understanding, such as the five false views of the view of a self, extreme views, false views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions; the delusion of thoughts is the ordinary person’s confusion and error in thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of beings’ birth and death and transmigration; cut them off, and one can put an end to birth and death and escape transmigration.

[The more you investigate, the more urgent it becomes; the more you rouse yourself, the more intimate it becomes. When your strength reaches its utmost and your practice is pure, suddenly the recitation falls away along with the one reciting, and you realize the state of no-thought and yet no absence of thought.]

The more one investigates, the finer and closer it becomes; the more one rouses oneself, the nearer one draws. When strength reaches its utmost and practice is pure, suddenly the grasped and the grasper both vanish, and one realizes the state of no-thought and yet no absence of thought.

[Strength at its utmost and practice pure] Strength brought to its farthest point, and practice utterly of one piece. [Suddenly] A phrase describing openness and thoroughness, as in “suddenly opened and bright,” “suddenly pierced through,” “suddenly awakened.” “Suddenly” also describes the look of awakening; for example, the Admonitions of the Yan Family: “What had been stagnant for years suddenly dissolved like fog.” Su Xun, First Letter to Ouyang Neihan: “When much time had passed and I read them more and more closely, my heart became suddenly clear.” [The recitation falls away along with the one reciting] The grasped and the grasper both vanish—the reciting mind and the recited Buddha fall away at one and the same moment.
Dissolved like fog
The fog disperses, a metaphor for the doubt-mass being completely cleared away.
There are several points to be heeded in cultivating Buddha-recitation-samādhi: 1. It is best to have some understanding of the true nature of all dharmas (see
Selected Annotations on the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury
for details
) and of the original nature (see
Mind, Self-Nature, Tathāgatagarbha
for details

) from the very beginning; 2. Whatever states may arise in the course of practice, one must neither accept nor cling to them, and only then can one advance; 3. Outside of sitting, one must temper the mind amid circumstances and not be turned by them, in order to realize the original nature through actual proof.

This essay describes how, having already attained the return of the ten thousand thoughts to one—“the whole of the recitation is contemplation, with no contemplation apart from the recitation; the whole of the contemplation is recitation, with no recitation apart from the contemplation”—one then uses the method of “investigating again and again” to realize the original nature directly. For students who have not yet attained the return of the ten thousand thoughts to one, the method of “investigating again and again” may likewise be used to attain it, and then to go further and attain the return of the one to nothing, and even to realize the original nature directly.

blocks.text: 4. Clarifying the Mind and Seeing the Nature

inline.s: [This is what is meant by the saying: “The luminous spirit shines alone, utterly freed from the faculties and their objects. Its essence is revealed as true and everlasting, and it is not bound by words. The mind-nature is undefiled and perfect from the very beginning; only let go of deluded thoughts, and you are the Tathāgata as such.”]

This passage borrows the words of the Chan Master Baizhang to describe the scene of seeing the original face directly (clarifying the mind and seeing the nature): the luminous spirit shines alone, and the six faculties and the six sense-objects drop away utterly (utterly freed from the faculties and their objects). The nature that is both true and everlasting appears clearly before one, and this cannot be described in words. Only then does one suddenly understand: the mind-nature is without any defilement or attachment and is perfect from the very beginning; one need only let go of deluded thoughts, and one is the dharmakāya Buddha. So this passage of Master Baizhang’s was speaking of precisely this scene!
[This is what is meant by the saying: “The luminous spirit shines alone, ... you are the Tathāgata as such”] So this passage of Master Baizhang’s was speaking of precisely this scene!
The Chan Master Baizhang, ascending the hall, said:

“The luminous spirit shines alone, utterly freed from the faculties and their objects. Its essence is revealed as true and everlasting, and it is not bound by words. The mind-nature is undefiled and perfect from the very beginning. Only let go of deluded conditions, and you are the Tathāgata as such.”
(The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source)

[Utterly freed from the faculties and their objects] The six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) are completely severed from the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas). [Deluded conditions] Falsely grasping at conditions; here “conditions” is a verb. [Only let go of deluded conditions, and you are the Tathāgata as such] One need only let go of deluded grasping at conditions, and one is the dharmakāya Buddha. The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says
: “The dharma-buddha
(the dharmakāya Buddha)
is beyond conditions.”
The Diamond Sūtra says:
“Away from all marks, one is named a buddha.”
[The Tathāgata as such] The Buddha who is awakened to the principle-body of suchness; that is, the dharmakāya Buddha. The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“What is the transformed Buddha? What is the reward-born Buddha? What is the Tathāgata as such?”
Master Hanshan said:

“When you look to the point where not a single thought arises, then past and future are cut off, and what lies between stands alone. Suddenly the black lacquer bucket is smashed, and you see the original face at once
(see the nature through and through)
. Then body and mind and the world sink away on the spot, like the phantoms of flowers in the sky fading
(the phantom flowers of the sky cease)

, and the ten directions are perfectly bright, forming one great treasury of radiance. Only thus is it the season of arriving home: as daily life unfolds before one, it is bright and perfectly clear, and there is nothing more to doubt. Only then does one believe that one’s own mind was like this from the very beginning. What the buddhas and patriarchs from of old enjoyed in their own experience is no different at all.”
Record of Dream Wanderings
Essential Pointers on Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation)

[Past and future limits] The past limit refers to the past, and the future limit refers to the future. The Jingying Commentary says: “Conditioned dharmas arise one after another. What precedes is the past limit, and what follows is the future limit.” [Severing past and future limits] To have neither a preceding thought nor a succeeding thought, that is, the state in which not a single thought is born. The Record of the Mirror of the Chan School says:

“Thus the Essentials of the Mind Commentary says: If not a single thought is born, then the past and future limits are severed. The luminescent essence stands alone; self and objects are both as-real, and one arrives directly at the source of mind.”
The Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan says:
“Hearing once, one awakens a thousand times and attains the great total-holding; when not a single thought is born, the past and future limits are severed.”
[Ping chen]
Also written “ping chen”: to sink into oblivion.
[When the effort reaches this point, the Buddha-recitation has been practiced aright, sympathetic resonance is established, and it is precisely the time to press on with vigor.]

When the effort reaches this point, the Buddha-recitation has been practiced in accord with the Dharma, and sympathetic resonance is established; it is exactly the time to press on with vigor and to ascend further.

[Its feature is like clouds dispersing from the vast sky, the blue heavens fully revealed, and one directly sees the origin. Fundamentally there is nothing to see; the absence of seeing is true seeing, while any seeing is to follow the sense-dust.]

When one directly sees the intrinsic nature, its feature is like clouds scattering across the vast sky, with the blue heavens fully revealed, and one directly sees the original face. Fundamentally there is nothing to be seen; absence of seeing is the real seeing, while any seeing means the sense-roots grasping the dust.
[Absence of seeing is true seeing] The intrinsic nature is formless; it can only be comprehended by spirit, hence it is said that “absence of seeing is true seeing.” The Diamond Sutra says:
“All conditioned appearances are all false and illusory.”
[Having seeing is to follow the dust] “Having seeing” means the sense-roots grasping the dust, for example the eye-root grasping form-dust or the mind-root grasping dharma-dust.

[Arriving at this point, the colors of the mountains and the sounds of the streams are all the truth of the First Meaning; the cawing of crows and the chatter of magpies are none other than the supreme true vehicle.]

Arriving at this point (having realized the essence), all scenes and objects — the colors of the mountains, the sounds of the streams, the caws of crows, the chirps of magpies — all manifest this absolute and inconceivable state: the colors of the mountains and the sounds of the streams are all the truth of the First Meaning (the true reality of all dharmas); the caws of the crows and the chirps of the magpies all proclaim the Dharma of the supreme true vehicle.
[The truth of the First Meaning] The supreme, unsurpassed truth — the true reality of all dharmas. The Buddha said:

“All dharmas are all false and illusory; where they cease, that is called real, that is called the true reality, that is called the dharma-realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the truth of the First Meaning, that is called the emptiness of the First Meaning.”
(From the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
Fascicle Forty.)
[Alive and vibrant, it responds to all dharmas yet abides in none; bright and luminous, it illumines all realms yet is utterly without a single thing.]
Alive and vibrant, it responds to all dharmas yet abides in none of them; bright and luminous, it reflects all realms yet in the mind there is utterly no single thing.
Master Hanshan said:

“If one sees the primordial awareness, then all forms, sounds, goods, and profits are clearly comprehended and no longer stir one. Meeting states and conditions in this way is like a mirror reflecting images — no single thing can move one.”
(From the Collected Wanderings in a Dream,
Instructions for Cao Shiju.)
[Speaking of its function, it is like the rising sun in the east — full and bright, illuminating all.]

Speaking of the function of directly seeing one's intrinsic nature, it is like the sun hanging in the sky: darkness is entirely dispelled, the pitfalls and the paths are clearly distinguished, and goblins and ghosts vanish away unnoticed.
[Pitfalls and passages] The pitfalls and the paths.

[Speaking of its essence, it is like the bright moon setting in the west — pure, clear, still, and extinguished. Luminous and still, still and luminous; both abiding and both vanishing, freed from all opposition and perfectly interfused.
